'''Ian Avrum Goldberg''' (born March 31, 1973) is a [[cryptographer]] and [[cypherpunk]]. He is best known for breaking [[Netscape Communications Corporation|Netscape's]] implementation of [[Secure Sockets Layer|SSL]] (with [[David A. Wagner|David Wagner]]),<ref name="netscape-ssl-cracked">
{{cite newsgroup
| author = Ian Goldberg
| date = 1995-09-18
| title = Netscape SSL implementation cracked!
| newsgroup = hks.lists.cypherpunks
| url = http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~daw/my-posts/netscape-cracked-0
| access-date = 2006-09-12
}}</ref> and for his role as chief scientist of Radialpoint (formerly [[Zero Knowledge Systems]]), a Canadian software company. Goldberg is currently a professor at the Faculty of Mathematics of the [[David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science]] within the [[University of Waterloo]], and the Canada Research Chair in Privacy Enhancing Technologies.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2022-01-10 |title=Privacy and cybersecurity can foster 21st Century democracy |url=https://uwaterloo.ca/news/global-impact/privacy-and-cybersecurity-can-foster-21st-century-democracy |access-date=2022-04-19 |website=Waterloo News |language=en}}</ref> He was formerly [[Tor (anonymity network)|Tor Project]] board of directors chairman,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/14/technology/tor-project-a-digital-privacy-group-reboots-with-new-board.html?_r=0 | title=Tor Project, a Digital Privacy Group, Reboots With New Board | newspaper=The New York Times | date=13 July 2016 | access-date=2016-07-13| last1=Perlroth | first1=Nicole }}</ref> and is one of the designers of [[off the record messaging]].<ref name="Tor Project Board of Directors">{{cite web |url=https://www.torproject.org/about/board.html.en |title=Tor Project Board of Directors |publisher=Tor Project |access-date=January 26, 2015}}</ref>

==Education==
Goldberg attended high school at the [[University of Toronto Schools]], graduating in 1991. In 1995, he received a [[Bachelor of Mathematics|BMath]] from the [[University of Waterloo]] in [[pure mathematics]] and computer science. He obtained a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in December 2000. His thesis was entitled ''A Pseudonymous Communications Infrastructure for the Internet''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.isaac.cs.berkeley.edu:80/~iang/thesis-final.pdf|title=A Pseudonymous Communications Infrastructure for the Internet|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011030065633/http://www.isaac.cs.berkeley.edu/~iang/thesis-final.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=30 October 2001|date=30 October 2001|access-date=5 February 2019}}</ref> His advisor was [[Eric Brewer (scientist)|Eric Brewer]].

==Accomplishments==
As a high school student, Goldberg was a member of Canada's team to the [[International Mathematical Olympiad|International Math Olympiad]] from 1989 to 1991, where he received a bronze, silver, and gold medal respectively.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imo-official.org/participant_r.aspx?id=1959|title=International Mathematical Olympiad: Hall of fame}}</ref> He was also a member of [[University of Waterloo]] team that won the [[ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest]] in 1994.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://icpc.baylor.edu/past/icpc94/Report.html|title=1993-94 18th Annual ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest Final Report|date=2002-04-01|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110102183152/http://icpc.baylor.edu/past/icpc94/Report.html|archive-date=2011-01-02}}</ref> In 1998, ''Wired'' Magazine chose him as a member of the "Wired 25".<ref name="wired-25">
{{cite magazine
| title = The Wired 25
| magazine = Wired
| volume = 6 | issue = 11
| date = November 1998
| url = https://www.wired.com/wired/archive/6.11/wired25.html?pg=10
| access-date = 2006-10-30
}}</ref>
In 2011 he won the [[EFF Pioneer Award]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2011/11/proud-recognize-effs-2011-pioneer-award-winners |title=EFF Celebrates the 2011 Pioneer Award Winners |date=18 November 2011 |access-date=10 December 2011}}</ref> In 2019, he won the [[USENIX]] Security Test of Time Award along with his colleagues David Wagner and Randi Thomas and former PhD supervisor Eric Brewer.<ref>{{cite web
| title = Ian Goldberg Colleagues Honoured Security Research Test of Time
| date = 14 August 2019
| url = https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/news/ian-goldberg-colleagues-honoured-security-research-test-of-time
| access-date = 2021-02-02
}}</ref> In 2023, he was named an [[ACM Fellow]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ian Goldberg |url=https://awards.acm.org/award-recipients/goldberg_4097200 |access-date=2024-01-26 |website=awards.acm.org |language=en}}</ref>

==Work in cryptography==
In 1995, Goldberg with [[David A. Wagner|David Wagner]] discovered a flaw in the [[random number generator]] used for temporary key generation in the SSL implementation of [[Netscape Navigator]].<ref name="netscape-ssl-cracked"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~daw/press/iang/ian1.html|title=The Cypherpunks Who Cracked Netscape|website=people.eecs.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

One of the first cryptanalyses on the [[Wired Equivalent Privacy|WEP]] wireless encryption protocol was conducted by Goldberg with [[Nikita Borisov]] and David Wagner, revealing serious flaws in its design.<ref name="wep-insecurity">
{{cite web
| author1=Nikita Borisov |author2=Ian Goldberg |author3=David Wagner | title = Intercepting Mobile Communications: The Insecurity of 802.11
| year = 2001
| url = http://www.isaac.cs.berkeley.edu/isaac/mobicom.pdf
| access-date = 2006-09-12
}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.isaac.cs.berkeley.edu/isaac/wep-faq.html|title=(In)Security of the WEP algorithm|website=www.isaac.cs.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

Goldberg was a co-author of the [[Off-the-Record Messaging|Off-the-Record]] [[instant messaging]] encryption protocol. He is also the author of the [[Perl]] script included in the novel ''[[Cryptonomicon]]'' by [[Neal Stephenson]].<ref name="Cryptonomicon">
{{Cite book
| author = Neal Stephenson
| title = ''Cryptonomicon''
| year = 1999
| publisher = Avon Books
| location = New York
| page = Acknowledgements
| isbn = 978-0-380-97346-0
| url-access = registration
| url = https://archive.org/details/cryptonomicon00step
}}</ref>

In 2009 Goldberg was co-author of the Sphinx Mix Format,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://cypherpunks.ca/~iang/pubs/Sphinx_Oakland09.pdf|title=Sphinx: A Compact and Provably Secure Mix Format|website=cypherpunks.ca/~iang/}}</ref> which is nowadays implemented with the extension of a per-hop payload to increase the privacy of both payer and payee while routing [[Bitcoin]] payments through the [[Lightning Network]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://github.com/lightningnetwork/lightning-rfc/blob/master/04-onion-routing.md|title=Basics Of Lightning Technology #4: Onion Routing Protocol|website=www.github.com/lightningnetwork/lightning-rfc|date=21 July 2022 }}</ref>

[[Vitalik Buterin]], co-founder of [[Ethereum]], was a research assistant of Goldberg while a student at the [[University of Waterloo]].<ref>{{cite magazine |date=13 July 2017 |title=The Uncanny Mind That Built Ethereum |url=https://www.wired.com/2016/06/the-uncanny-mind-that-built-ethereum/ |magazine=Wired |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170713184159/https://www.wired.com/2016/06/the-uncanny-mind-that-built-ethereum/ |archive-date=2017-07-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Hitt |first=Tarpley |date=2021-05-05 |title=Meet the World's Youngest Crypto Billionaire |language=en |work=The Daily Beast |url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/meet-vitalik-buterin-the-worlds-youngest-crypto-billionaire-ethereum-founder |access-date=2022-04-19}}</ref>

Goldberg is a member of the Cryptography, Security and Privacy group as well as the Cybersecurity and Privacy Institute (CPI). He has been collaborating with the CPI works on the development of a new interdisciplinary research and education program.<ref name=":0" />
